        <title><![CDATA[Evaluating the role of craniocervical and atlantoaxial instability in autonomic dysfunction: a narrative review]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-26T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Review</category>
        <author>Louis Vilotti</author><author>Nicholas DePace</author><author>Joseph Colombo</author><author>Adam Benn</author>
        <description><![CDATA[BackgroundAutonomic dysfunction is a complex condition that affects every organ system in the body. The underlying mechanisms of autonomic dysfunction remain incompletely understood. There appears to be an association between patients with hypermobile Ehlers Danlos syndrome (hEDS), craniocervical instability (CCI), atlantoaxial instability (AAI), and autonomic dysfunction. There is biological plausibility for CCI and AAI being causes for autonomic dysfunction in these populations.ObjectiveThe objective of this review is to explore the literature on the potential association between CCI, AAI and autonomic dysfunction and to explore the biological plausibility of this association.MethodsA narrative review of PubMed was conducted through August 2026 to evaluate associations among hEDS, CCI/AAI, and autonomic dysfunction. Studies addressing autonomic dysfunction in hypermobility disorders, CCI/AAI, autonomic outcomes following cervical stabilization surgeries, and proposed neurovascular or autonomic mechanisms were included. Findings were synthesized narratively due to the heterogeneity of the study designs analyzed and outcome measures assessed.Results43 studies were included in the final review. Evidence consistently supported an association between hEDS and autonomic dysfunction and between hEDS and CCI/AAI. More limited evidence demonstrated a direct overlap between CCI/AAI and dysautonomia, while multiple series reports showed improvements in autonomic-associated symptoms following surgical stabilization procedures. Proposed mechanisms for autonomic dysfunction in CCI/AAI patients include vagal nerve involvement, internal jugular vein compression, altered cerebral venous outflow, and cervicomedullary effects. The evidence was predominantly retrospective and heterogeneous, with limited standardized autonomic testing, warranting further investigation and more robust future analysis.ConclusionCurrent evidence suggests that CCI and AAI represent under-recognized contributors to dysautonomia. While causality has not been established, anatomical, physiological, and clinical observations warrant further investigation into this relationship. Standardized diagnostic criteria for CCI/AAI, as well as autonomic dysfunction, must be established to further study these relationships. Prospective studies incorporating these diagnostic criteria and objective autonomic measurements will assist in clarifying these relationships and determine what interventions will help improve patient outcomes.]]></description>

        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1966414</guid>

        <title><![CDATA[Effect of ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block on intraoperative hemodynamics in laparoscopic partial adrenalectomy: a randomized clinical trial]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-26T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Original Research</category>
        <author>Jingyi Nie</author><author>Huang Wang</author><author>Wenjing Zhang</author><author>Hui Wang</author><author>Pengqian Hao</author><author>Junchai Liu</author><author>Jiwen Shang</author><author>Weiwei Zhang</author>
        <description><![CDATA[PurposeThis study aimed to evaluate the effect of ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block (SGB) on intraoperative hemodynamic parameters in patients undergoing laparoscopic partial adrenalectomy.Patients and methodsA total of 72 patients with adrenal tumors scheduled for laparoscopic partial adrenalectomy were enrolled and randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the stellate ganglion block (SGB) group or the control group. The primary outcome was the incidence of intraoperative hypertension, defined as a systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥180 mmHg or an increase of ≥30% in mean arterial pressure (MAP) from baseline. Secondary outcomes included MAP and heart rate (HR) measured at nine predefined perioperative time points, intraoperative vasoactive drug consumption, and the incidence of perioperative adverse events.ResultsThe incidence of intraoperative hypertension was significantly lower in the SGB group than in the control group (14.3% vs. 37.1%, p = 0.029). Compared with the control group, patients in the SGB group exhibited significantly lower MAP and HR at eight time points ranging from immediately after tracheal intubation until the end of surgery (p < 0.05). The intraoperative consumption of phentolamine was significantly lower in the SGB group than in the control group [0 (0–4) mg vs. 0 (0–0) mg; p = 0.008]. In contrast, the consumption of norepinephrine was significantly higher in the SGB group [0 (0–0) mg vs. 0 (0–8) mg; p = 0.004]. No statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups in the consumption of esmolol and atropine, or in the incidence of perioperative adverse events.ConclusionUltrasound-guided SGB lowers intraoperative hypertension incidence and phentolamine demand in laparoscopic partial adrenalectomy. Although the SGB group observed a slight increase in the intraoperative dose of norepinephrine, no perioperative adverse events occurred. There was also no significant difference in the incidence of adverse reactions between the two groups.]]></description>
      </item><item>
        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1973784</guid>
        <link>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1973784</link>
        <title><![CDATA[ECG Holter-based screening for sleep-disordered breathing in post-stroke patients: a large monocentric cohort study]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-26T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Original Research</category>
        <author>Mathilde Monier</author><author>Vincent Pichot</author><author>Mathieu Berger</author><author>Béatrice Trombert</author><author>Pierre Garnier</author><author>Jean-Philippe Camdessanché</author><author>Frédéric Roche</author>
        <description><![CDATA[IntroductionSleep-disordered breathing (SDB) is highly prevalent after stroke and is associated with poor functional outcomes and increased mortality, yet systematic screening remains challenging because of limited polysomnography accessibility. We evaluated three electrocardiogram (ECG)-based indices for SDB screening in a large consecutive post-stroke cohort.MethodsThis retrospective single-centre cohort study included 1,929 consecutive patients hospitalised for stroke or transient ischaemic attack at Saint-Étienne University Hospital (2010–2021) who were in sinus rhythm with ECG signal quality adequate for ECG-derived respiration (EDR) analysis; patients with atrial fibrillation, pacemaker rhythm, or severe ectopy (>10% of beats) were excluded a priori. EDR, the Thoracic Impedance Disturbance Index (TIDI) and the Very Low Frequency Increment (VLFI) were compared with the simultaneous oxygen desaturation index (ODI) as reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity, accuracy and predictive values were calculated at ODI thresholds of 15/h and 30/h; a combined TIDI+EDR concordant rule was assessed as a post-hoc exploratory analysis.ResultsThe cohort comprised 61% males (mean age 65.9 years). Suspected SDB (ODI ≥ 5/h) was present in 74.6% of patients, moderate-to-severe SDB (ODI ≥ 15/h) in 38.9% and severe SDB (ODI ≥ 30/h) in 17.1%. For ODI ≥ 15/h (n = 750), TIDI had the highest sensitivity (93.3%) and negative predictive value (90.8%), whereas EDR had higher specificity (80.2%) and accuracy (74.2%); the combined rule reached 85.2% specificity and 72.9% positive predictive value. For ODI ≥ 30/h (n = 330), EDR showed specificity of 92.4% and accuracy of 85.2%, and the combined rule 95.4% and 86.9%, respectively. VLFI performed poorly across all metrics.DiscussionECG-based tools can identify post-stroke patients at high risk of SDB using routine cardiac monitoring. The complementary profiles of TIDI (rule-out) and EDR (rule-in) support a sequential screening approach, which requires prospective validation against polysomnography. VLFI is unsuitable for elderly stroke populations because of age-related autonomic dysfunction. Because patients with atrial fibrillation, pacemaker rhythm or severe arrhythmia were excluded, the findings may not generalise to this higher-arrhythmia-burden subgroup, who may also be at higher risk of SDB.]]></description>
      </item><item>
        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1929675</guid>
        <link>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1929675</link>
        <title><![CDATA[Case Report: Cerebral air embolism following fluid–air exchange during pars plana vitrectomy: a rare but severe complication]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-26T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Case Report</category>
        <author>Rong Zhang</author><author>Guo Wen</author><author>Zhenqun Zhang</author>
        <description><![CDATA[Cerebral air embolism (CAE) is a rare but potentially life-threatening neurological emergency, typically caused by the inadvertent entry of exogenous air into the venous circulation and subsequent migration to the cerebral vasculature. It presents with abrupt onset and a prognosis that heavily depends on early recognition and prompt intervention. We report a case of CAE that occurred during pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) involving intraoperative fluid–air exchange. The patient experienced sudden ocular pain intraoperatively, followed shortly post-operatively by acute neurological symptoms including altered consciousness, ataxia, and slurred speech. Brain MRI using a standard stroke protocol, including DWI with b values of 0 and 1,000 s/mm2 and ADC maps, revealed multiple acute infarcts in the bilateral frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes, thalamus, and corpus callosum. DWI demonstrated widespread hyperintensity with corresponding ADC reduction. Although no definite intravascular air artifacts were detected, the combination of intraoperative pressure fluctuations, a hypercoagulable state, and elevated levels of D-dimer and cardiac troponin I strongly supported the diagnosis of CAE with possible concomitant microembolism-induced ischemia. The patient received prompt multidisciplinary intensive care and exhibited marked neurological recovery with favorable prognosis. This case highlights the need for high clinical suspicion of CAE during procedures involving air infusion, abrupt pressure changes, or vascular injury risk. Emergent neuroimaging and multidisciplinary management are critical to minimizing neurological sequelae and ensuring patient safety.]]></description>
      </item><item>
        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1989720</guid>
        <link>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1989720</link>
        <title><![CDATA[Hyperhomocysteinemia and Klotho in kidney-to-brain signaling: a metabolic stress-resilience framework for neurovascular dysfunction]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-26T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Review</category>
        <author>Dongyan Zhou</author><author>Yulong Zhao</author><author>Yanjian Zheng</author><author>Jianying Xu</author><author>Bibo Xie</author><author>Yuqiu Zhou</author><author>Yingpin Zhang</author>
        <description><![CDATA[Hyperhomocysteinemia (HHcy) and Klotho deficiency are commonly investigated in separate metabolic, renal, vascular, and neurological contexts, yet together they may illuminate how peripheral dysfunction is translated into cerebral vulnerability. This review develops a kidney-to-brain stress resilience framework in which HHcy represents a renal dysfunction-associated component of systemic metabolic and vascular stress, whereas α-Klotho represents a candidate indicator of biological resilience, supported mainly by experimental evidence and observational human studies. Declining renal function favors Hcy accumulation, reduces renal Klotho expression, and generates uremic, inflammatory, mineral, and hemodynamic disturbances that converge on the cerebral microvasculature. Experimental HHcy can additionally repress renal KL through HDAC9-dependent epigenetic regulation. At the brain-facing interface, circulating Hcy directly disrupts cerebral endothelial bioenergetics, redox homeostasis, inflammatory signaling, and tight-junction integrity, providing a plausible route from systemic metabolic disturbance to blood–brain barrier (BBB) and neurovascular-unit (NVU) dysfunction. Klotho-related mechanisms, in contrast, are associated with endothelial, antioxidant, mitochondrial, anti-inflammatory, and anti-senescent resilience, although circulating, renal, and CNS Klotho represent non-equivalent compartments and the causal contribution of circulating Klotho to human neurological disease remains uncertain. Clinical and imaging evidence from chronic kidney disease, cerebral small-vessel disease (CSVD), cognitive impairment, and ischemic stroke supports individual components of the proposed kidney circulation BBB/NVU brain continuum, but not a validated linear HHcy-Klotho molecular axis. We therefore define HHcy-high/Klotho-low status as a candidate metabolic stress-resilience phenotype and propose that the critical test is whether Klotho modifies the neurovascular consequences of a given Hcy burden. Establishing this framework will require cell-specific perturbation, compartment-resolved Klotho measurement, longitudinal neuroimaging, and prospective analyses linking renal dysfunction, BBB/NVU injury, CSVD progression, and cognitive decline.]]></description>
      </item><item>
        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1833413</guid>
        <link>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1833413</link>
        <title><![CDATA[Gene expression analysis of Fmr1-KO mouse caudate putamen reveals new preclinical biomarkers for fragile X syndrome]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-23T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Original Research</category>
        <author>Shirin Sharghi</author><author>Stefanie Flunkert</author><author>Magdalena Daurer</author><author>Livia Breznik</author><author>Boris Philippe Chagnaud</author><author>Manuela Prokesch</author>
        <description><![CDATA[BackgroundFragile X syndrome is a monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder. Fmr1-KO mice are a well-known model for the disease, and the model’s behavioral phenotype has been well-characterized. Unfortunately, translational molecular tissue biomarkers for this model remain sparse.MethodsTo identify new molecular biomarkers, we performed a gene sequencing analysis of caudate putamen tissue of Fmr1-KO mice at the age of 7 weeks. RNA sequencing analysis revealed 13 genes to be upregulated and 37 genes to be downregulated in the caudate putamen of Fmr1-KO mice. The two most upregulated genes were necdin (Ndn) and insulin degrading enzyme (Ide). Upregulation of Ndn and Ide genes was confirmed by real-time PCR. NDN protein expression was analyzed in the caudate putamen, hippocampus, and brainstem using immunofluorescent labeling. A co-labeling experiment assessed NDN expression in cholinergic neurons. Ide gene upregulation and its effect on insulin levels were evaluated, and protein expression analysis focused on NDN, parvalbumin, and myelin basic protein in the caudate putamen, cortex, and hippocampus.ResultsmRNA levels of Ndn and Ide and protein levels of NDN and IDE were strongly upregulated in the caudate putamen of Fmr1-KO mice. NDN protein expression was also increased in the hippocampus and brainstem, with partial expression observed in cholinergic neurons. Upregulated Ide gene expression was associated with reduced insulin levels in Fmr1-KO mice.ConclusionNDN and IDE emerge as promising candidates for preclinical disease-relevant biomarkers in Fmr1-KO mice. Future research needs to demonstrate whether disease-modulating drugs can alter the expression profile of these proteins and ultimately alleviate disease symptoms.]]></description>
      </item><item>
        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1976324</guid>
        <link>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1976324</link>
        <title><![CDATA[Comparison of short-term peripheral nerve stimulation, single-target supraorbital nerve pulsed radiofrequency, and dual-target supraorbital nerve–stellate ganglion pulsed radiofrequency for herpes zoster ophthalmicus–associated pain: a retrospective cohort study]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-23T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Original Research</category>
        <author>Chen Liang</author><author>Anxiang Liu</author><author>Wei Wang</author>
        <description><![CDATA[ObjectiveTo compare the clinical outcomes of short-term peripheral nerve stimulation (st-PNS), supraorbital nerve pulsed radiofrequency (SON-PRF), and combined supraorbital nerve and stellate ganglion pulsed radiofrequency (SON + SG-PRF) for herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO)-associated pain.MethodsThis retrospective study included patients with HZO-associated pain who underwent st-PNS, SON-PRF, or SON + SG-PRF between January 2023 and January 2026. The primary outcome was the longitudinal change in Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) scores over 24 weeks. Secondary outcomes included the clinical response rate, anxiety (GAD-7), depression (PHQ-9), sleep quality (PSQI), and treatment-related adverse events. The incidence of postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) was assessed as an exploratory outcome only in patients with a disease duration of ≤90 days at treatment. Longitudinal outcomes were analyzed using baseline-adjusted linear mixed-effects models, with propensity score weighting used for sensitivity analyses.ResultsA total of 269 patients were included: 84 in the st-PNS group, 96 in the SON-PRF group, and 89 in the SON + SG-PRF group. NRS scores decreased over follow-up in all three groups. In the primary and both propensity score-weighted analyses, the overall NRS trajectory was lower with st-PNS than with SON-PRF, whereas no significant difference was observed between st-PNS and SON + SG-PRF. The overall GAD-7 trajectory was lower with SON + SG-PRF than with SON-PRF, and the overall PSQI trajectory was lower with SON + SG-PRF than with either st-PNS or SON-PRF; these differences remained statistically significant in both weighted analyses. The overall trajectories of depressive symptoms did not differ significantly among the groups. Exploratory analysis did not establish a difference in PHN risk among the three groups. No serious treatment-related adverse events occurred during follow-up.ConclusionTo our knowledge, this study is the first to compare multidimensional clinical outcomes of st-PNS, SON-PRF, and SON + SG-PRF for HZO-associated pain within the same cohort. st-PNS showed a relatively consistent analgesic benefit over SON-PRF, whereas SON + SG-PRF also provided analgesia and showed potential benefits for anxiety and sleep outcomes. These findings require confirmation in prospective studies.]]></description>
      </item><item>
        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1844932</guid>
        <link>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1844932</link>
        <title><![CDATA[Research progress on the mechanism of microglia–astrocyte signal crosstalk in central sensitization of vestibular migraine]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-23T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Review</category>
        <author>Tiancan Jin</author><author>Weitao Wang</author><author>Jinghan Qin</author><author>Yaru Liu</author><author>Xiaofei Fan</author><author>Daopei Zhang</author><author>Huailiang Zhang</author>
        <description><![CDATA[Vestibular migraine (VM) is a vestibular disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of vertigo, frequently accompanied by headache, nausea, and vomiting, which substantially reduce patients’ quality of life. The pathogenesis of VM remains incompletely understood. Current studies mainly focus on ion channel dysfunction, trigeminovascular mechanisms, and genetic susceptibility. Increasing evidence suggests that neuroinflammation and central sensitization play important roles in the onset and maintenance of VM. Microglia and astrocytes are key mediators of central sensitization, and their bidirectional communication represents an important component of neuroimmune interactions in the central nervous system. Based on recent studies, this review systematically summarizes the interactions and crosstalk between microglia and astrocytes in central sensitization, aiming to provide further insight into the pathophysiology of VM and to explore potential preventive and therapeutic strategies.]]></description>
      </item><item>
        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1962306</guid>
        <link>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1962306</link>
        <title><![CDATA[Continuous performance tests in the assessment of children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a narrative review]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-22T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Review</category>
        <author>Yao Zhou</author><author>Xiaoke Zhao</author>
        <description><![CDATA[Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is diagnosed primarily through clinical interviews, behavioral observations, and rating scales, while continuous performance tests (CPTs) provide complementary, performance-based measures of sustained attention, response inhibition, and response consistency. This narrative review compares major CPT paradigms used in pediatric ADHD assessment according to their cognitive targets, task characteristics, psychometric properties, ecological validity, clinical applications, and evidence maturity. Traditional standardized paradigms generally provide more established normative and psychometric frameworks, with the strongest support available for the Conners CPT series and TOVA, whereas distraction-enhanced, motion-integrated, virtual reality-based, and eye-tracking-integrated approaches extend assessment toward more complex and ecologically relevant behavioral contexts. Evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses supports group-level differences in core CPT measures, particularly reaction time variability, omission errors, and commission errors; however, substantial overlap across ADHD, psychiatric comorbidities, developmental stages, and other clinical conditions limits their specificity for individual diagnosis. Technology-enhanced paradigms may provide additional information regarding distractibility, motor activity, and gaze behavior, but their incremental clinical value remains uncertain because of heterogeneous methodologies, limited independent replication, and insufficient large-scale cross-cultural normative data. CPTs should therefore be interpreted as objective adjuncts within a multimodal assessment framework rather than as standalone diagnostic or subtype-classification tools. Future research should prioritize standardized outcome definitions, age-appropriate normative datasets, management of practice effects in repeated testing, and prospective multicenter studies evaluating whether specific CPT paradigms add clinically meaningful information beyond established diagnostic and treatment-monitoring procedures.]]></description>
      </item><item>
        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1902749</guid>
        <link>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1902749</link>
        <title><![CDATA[Striatal and orbitofrontal grey matter volumes are associated with cognitive event related potentials during associative learning task performance in male and female children and adolescents]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-22T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Original Research</category>
        <author>Kymbat Kassen</author><author>Rassul Shakhzadayev</author><author>Manzura Zholdassova</author><author>Oxana Kabenova</author><author>Altyngul Kamzanova</author><author>Gaukhar Datkhabayeva</author><author>Daniyar Abdilmanov</author><author>Jane B. Allendorfer</author><author>James Eliassen</author><author>Mikhail Ye. Mel’nikov</author><author>Almira Kustubayeva</author>
        <description><![CDATA[IntroductionThe individual differences in gray matter volumes and event-related potentials may underlie variability in associative learning. However, little is known about the sex differences in these structure–function relationships across development.MethodsThe current study investigates associations between local gray matter volumes and brain responses during associative learning task in children and adolescents aged 7–21 years. We hypothesized that gray matter volumes of the basal ganglia and prefrontal cortex would be associated with event-related potentials indices of associative learning, in a sex-dependent manner. Final analysis included 138 participants (68 females, 70 males). Participants completed an associative learning task with concurrent EEG event-related potentials recording. Gray matter volumes were analyzed within 5 a priori regions of interest, predominantly located in the basal ganglia vicinity and prefrontal cortex.ResultsIn females, anterior N400 latency to Early-stage stimulus onsets was positively associated with gray matter volume in the left putamen/lentiform nucleus and to Late-stage stimulus onsets with gray matter volume in the subgenual anterior cingulate. Anterior P300 amplitude to Late-stage feedback presentation was positively associated with gray matter volume in the right nucleus accumbens/putamen and the right medial orbitofrontal cortex. Correlations involving the subgenual anterior cingulate and medial orbitofrontal cortex were significantly stronger in the female group relative to the male group. In males, anterior P300 amplitude to Early-stage feedback presentation was associated with gray matter volume in a left hippocampus/amygdala cluster, yet not significantly differently from females. In exploratory analysis, after accounting for total brain volumes, age was positively associated with the volumes of striatal and orbitofrontal regions in both sexes, with largely overlapping patterns.DiscussionTherefore, findings support structure–function relationships linking gray matter volumes of striatum and orbitofrontal cortex to brain activity during reinforcement learning performance. Given that associative learning is an instance of reinforcement learning, its underlying neural processes are influenced by the structural development of striatal and orbitofrontal regions.]]></description>
      </item><item>
        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.2007175</guid>
        <link>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.2007175</link>
        <title><![CDATA[Microglia in the neurogenic niche: emerging roles of immunometabolism]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-22T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Mini Review</category>
        <author>Danping Liu</author><author>Yunjun Li</author><author>Yan Liu</author>
        <description><![CDATA[Adult neurogenesis is dynamically regulated by the neurogenic niche, yet the mechanisms governing its remodeling are not fully elucidated. Current research has increasingly extended beyond the intrinsic properties of neural stem cells to consider the broader microenvironment in which neurogenesis occurs, with microglia emerging as important regulators of the neurogenic niche. Drawing upon pathological contexts such as depression and aging, this review characterizes the hallmarks of neurogenic niche dysregulation and synthesizes the mechanisms by which microglia modulate neurogenic efficiency. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of immunometabolism in shaping microglial functional states and subsequent niche remodeling. We propose that microglial immunometabolic states may serve as an important interface through which pathological perturbations within the brain are linked to remodeling of the neurogenic niche, providing a conceptual framework for understanding neurogenic decline across distinct pathological contexts.]]></description>
      </item><item>
        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1923279</guid>
        <link>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1923279</link>
        <title><![CDATA[The mammalian regulatory architecture: biobehavioral portals and the organization of physiological state]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-22T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Hypothesis and Theory</category>
        <author>Stephen W. Porges</author>
        <description><![CDATA[IntroductionNeuromodulatory interventions can produce overlapping adaptive outcomes despite engaging substantially different biological pathways. Pathway-centered approaches identify how interventions initially engage the nervous system and characterize pathway-specific mechanisms. Convergence across interventions raises an additional question: how can different biological routes influence overlapping domains of adaptive function?MethodsThis conceptual paper develops the Mammalian Regulatory Architecture (MRA), an organizational framework informed by identified mammalian synapomorphies (shared derived characteristics) and comparative anatomical, developmental, physiological, and functional observations.ResultsThe MRA hypothesizes that mammalian evolution reorganized relationships among conserved regulatory processes through their integration with mammalian specializations and regulatory demands associated with nursing, prolonged developmental dependency, caregiving, co-regulation, and reciprocal social communication. The framework provides the basis for a biological portal model of neuromodulation that distinguishes the pathway of initial engagement from the functional significance of that engagement within the broader regulatory architecture. Whereas the pathway identifies how an intervention initially engages the nervous system, its portal significance concerns how that engagement influences state-regulating processes within the MRA.DiscussionThe proposed framework reframes neuromodulation from a process defined primarily by its neural target or pathway to one in which pathway engagement may influence broader regulatory organization, physiological state, Accessibility—the state-dependent availability of existing adaptive capacities—and adaptive function. It offers an organizational account of how distinct biological routes may influence overlapping domains of adaptive function.]]></description>
      </item><item>
        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1940267</guid>
        <link>https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1940267</link>
        <title><![CDATA[Overcoming subject variability in P300 decoding based on quantification by deep learning]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-22T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Original Research</category>
        <author>Maohua Liu</author><author>Fred R. Beyette</author>
        <description><![CDATA[Binary P300 decoding is a cornerstone of P300-based brain-computer interfaces, enabling applications such as assistive communication, neurorehabilitation, and cognitive monitoring. However, substantial subject variability in EEG patterns poses a major challenge to the development of generalized P300 decoders. To address this problem, this study proposes SQ_EMoE, a subject-variability-aware enhanced Mixture-of-Experts framework that uses the confidence produced by a deep subject-identification network as a practical proxy for trial-level subject distinctiveness. High-confidence trials are routed to subject-specific experts, whereas uncertain trials are redirected to a pooled general expert, allowing the framework to dynamically balance subject-specific specialization and cross-subject generalization. Latent subject representations are further visualized to qualitatively examine subject separability and its relationship with routing behavior. Experiments on eight random subjects from each of two public P300 datasets yielded mean ROC–AUC values of approximately 0.86 on BNCI Horizon 2020 and 0.89 on P300-LINI, outperforming pooled EEGNet and architecture-matched pooled P300MCNN baselines. Ablation experiments further demonstrated the contribution of confidence-controlled fallback to the general expert. To evaluate scalability, the framework was additionally tested on all 22 subjects of P300-LINI. With the original subject-identification network, SQ_EMoE achieved a mean ROC–AUC of 0.8518; after strengthening the subject representation and identification network, performance increased to 0.8760, exceeding the pooled P300MCNN baseline (0.8482) and slightly surpassing the oracle routing or within-subject decoding (0.8744). Leave-one-subject-out experiments further showed that the under-realized SQ_EMoE conservatively redirects most completely unseen-subject trials to the general expert when reliable subject-specific routing is unavailable. These results demonstrate that effective modeling of subject variability, together with adaptive integration of shared and subject-specific representations, provides a promising alternative to conventional one-size-fits-all EEG decoding.]]></description>
      </item><item>
        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1843917</guid>

        <title><![CDATA[Multiparametric MRI radiomics and machine learning for outcome prediction in acute ischemic stroke: a retrospective study of 353 patients]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-22T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Original Research</category>
        <author>Xiaoxing Peng</author><author>Jiannan Guo</author><author>Qiuyan Zhou</author><author>Shunyu Wang</author><author>Tingting Li</author>
        <description><![CDATA[BackgroundAcute ischemic stroke (AIS) remains a leading cause of death and disability worldwide. Early prediction for clinical outcomes is essential for guiding therapy. Multiparametric Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) offers detailed characterization of ischemic tissue and may predict prognosis in AIS patients. This study assesses the prognostic value of multiparametric MRI parameters in predicting functional outcome, recurrence risk and mortality in AIS patients.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective analysis of 353 AIS patients who underwent multiparametric MRI within 24 h of onset. MRI metrics including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) lesion volume, ADC minimum, perfusion parameters and Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging (SWI) microbleeds were correlated with National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) and modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores at discharge and 90 days. Predictive performance for clinical outcomes was assessed by receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) analysis.ResultsAmong 353 AIS patients with a mean door-to-imaging time of 27 ± 10 min, higher NIHSS, larger DWI volume, prolonged mean transit time (MTT) and Tmax, and increased microbleeds significantly correlated with mortality and disability, while lower ADC, CBF, and CBV correlated inversely with clinical outcomes. NIHSS ≥10.5 and DWI lesion volume ≥52.5 mL yielded AUCs of 0.963 and 0.975 and accuracies of 91.35% and 92.79%, respectively; CBF ≤ 20.5 yielded an AUC of 0.975. NIHSS ≥8.5 and MTT ≥8.5 s showed AUCs of 0.948 and 0.931, respectively, for predicting hemorrhagic transformation. Perfusion thresholds modestly predicted 90-day recurrence (AUC = 0.7). Hypertension, diabetes, and prior stroke were significant clinical predictors of poor outcome. These predictive metrics reflect internal, within-cohort validation only; independent external validation is required before clinical application.ConclusionMultiparametric MRI provides robust prognostic information in AIS. Quantitative thresholds for perfusion and diffusion parameters help in risk stratification for hemorrhage and mortality, enhancing individualized management and outcome prediction.]]></description>

        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1978796</guid>

        <title><![CDATA[Poststroke sleep phenotypes and executive dysfunction: toward a sleep-network-executive framework]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-21T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Hypothesis and Theory</category>
        <author>Jincheng Xu</author><author>Yan Zhang</author><author>Dandan Lin</author><author>Xue Yan</author><author>Nanyun Xie</author><author>Sutao Si</author><author>Shuming Yang</author>
        <description><![CDATA[Post-stroke sleep disturbance and executive dysfunction frequently coexist, yet the mechanisms linking disturbed sleep to cognitive recovery remain poorly understood. A major challenge is phenotypic heterogeneity: insomnia, sleep fragmentation, obstructive sleep apnea, hypersomnolence, and circadian disruption differ in their biological drivers and cognitive consequences. To develop a testable network-level account, we conducted a targeted synthesis of clinical stroke studies, stroke neuroimaging research, non-stroke sleep-network evidence, and intervention studies, mapping each evidence stream according to its proximity to the proposed pathway. The synthesis indicates that focal lesions, diaschisis, and structural disconnection after stroke can disrupt the integrity and coordination of the salience, default mode, and frontoparietal networks. Clinical studies support an association between disturbed sleep and poorer post-stroke cognition, while neuroimaging findings demonstrate altered large scale network organization in post-stroke cognitive impairment. Evidence from non-stroke populations further suggests that sleep loss, insomnia, and sleep fragmentation can impair network segregation, default mode regulation, frontoparietal recruitment, and salience-network-mediated switching. We therefore propose that sleep fragmentation, insomnia, and arousal instability may act as functional stressors on an already vulnerable post-stroke network architecture. Inefficient switching may permit context-inappropriate persistence of default mode activity and reduce or delay frontoparietal engagement during executive demand, thereby contributing to impaired conflict monitoring, working memory, processing speed, and cognitive flexibility. No study has directly tested this complete pathway within a single stroke cohort. The framework should therefore be regarded as a falsifiable mechanistic hypothesis rather than an established causal model. Future studies should combine objective sleep phenotyping, dynamic and effective connectivity, task based neuroimaging, domain specific executive measures, and longitudinal or interventional designs within the same stroke cohorts.]]></description>

        <title><![CDATA[Three-dimensional in vitro models for assessing temozolomide sensitivity in glioblastoma]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-21T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Review</category>
        <author>Andresa Hiromi Sakai</author><author>Marna Eliana Sakalem</author><author>Luiza Magosso Oliveira Rocha</author><author>Isabely Mayara da Silva</author><author>Flávia Eliza Staut Silva</author><author>Diego Luís Ribeiro</author><author>Carlos Frederico Martins Menck</author><author>Helber Alves Negreiros</author><author>João Marcelo de Castro e Sousa</author><author>Juliana Mara Serpeloni</author>
        <description><![CDATA[IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, or glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), is the most aggressive primary malignancy of the central nervous system. It is characterized by marked invasiveness, intratumoral heterogeneity, and high recurrence rates, largely driven by intrinsic and acquired resistance to standard temozolomide (TMZ) therapy. TMZ is an oral alkylating agent that methylates nitrogenous bases, mainly forming O6-methylguanine (O6-meG) lesions, the main cytotoxic and mutagenic events responsible for its antitumor effects. This review first characterizes gliomas and the mechanism of action of the main GBM treatment drug (TMZ), then critically examines in vitro cell culture models investigating these mechanisms. This review emphasizes the development and application of three-dimensional (3D) culture systems, including tumor spheroids and organoids, which more effectively recapitulate tumor architecture, cell–cell interactions, and drug penetration gradients than conventional two-dimensional models. This review discusses the strengths and limitations of these models and their translational relevance to modeling TMZ sensitivity and resistance in GBM.]]></description>

        <title><![CDATA[The perioperative sensory–cognitive interface: multimodal neuroimaging of hierarchical network reconfiguration in perioperative neurocognitive disorders]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-21T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Review</category>
        <author>Nanbo Luo</author><author>Zhengjun Liu</author><author>Zhiheng Liu</author>
        <description><![CDATA[Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PNDs) are commonly attributed to neuroinflammation, cerebrovascular stress, anesthetic neurophysiology, and pre-existing brain vulnerability. These mechanisms identify important insults but do not fully explain how they become disturbances of attention, perception, memory, executive control, and fluctuating awareness. We examine whether changes at the sensory–cognitive interface help explain these symptoms, focusing on postoperative delirium (POD) and early recovery within the broader PND classification. The interface comprises distributed, bidirectional operations that transform sensory evidence into context-sensitive representations through thalamocortical routing, integration, attention, and association systems. The framework makes three testable predictions: sensory function should add explanatory value beyond frailty and brain burden; perioperative effects should vary across hierarchical levels and time rather than reflect uniform suppression; and within-person recovery trajectories should explain outcome better than isolated scans. Anesthetic state-transition studies show that primary sensory responses can persist while feedback, thalamic broadcasting, and distributed integration are disrupted, but whether these changes cause PND remains unproven. Direct perioperative MRI and EEG studies identify pre-existing dysconnectivity, altered sensory and association-network organization, abnormal slow-wave and auditory-feedback dynamics, and incomplete postoperative recovery; nevertheless, findings are heterogeneous and sensory-specific tasks remain uncommon. These observations are compatible with established vulnerability–perturbation models and suggest that symptoms may depend on which networks recover and when. Structural–functional connectivity (SC–FC) coupling is one candidate measurement, not an established biomarker or a requirement of the framework. Longitudinal studies integrating sensory phenotyping, domain-specific cognition, delirium surveillance, MRI, EEG, physiology, and molecular markers should test whether this framework adds reproducible value beyond vascular injury, diffuse arousal failure, and latent neurodegeneration.]]></description>

        <title><![CDATA[Role of astrocytes in obesity-induced hypertension]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-21T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Review</category>
        <author>Diani Nanayakkara</author><author>Claudia Pantoja Negron</author><author>Madhan Subramanian</author>
        <description><![CDATA[Although obesity is a significant contributor to hypertension and cardiovascular disease, the mechanisms that connect excess adiposity to persistently elevated blood pressure extend far beyond peripheral metabolic and vascular changes. An increasing body of evidence suggests that a substantial component of this puzzle is disrupted autonomic regulation, specifically persistent activation of sympathetic pathways. This review explores the emerging role astrocytes play in this process. By controlling extracellular glutamate, ion balance, inflammatory signaling, energy metabolism, blood brain barrier integrity and neurovascular coupling, astrocytes normally contribute to the maintenance of neuronal and vascular homeostasis. However, exposure to excess nutrients, circulating fatty acids, adipokines and inflammatory mediators can interfere with these processes and cause astrocytes to become reactive. This change may increase oxidative and inflammatory signaling, hinder glutamate clearance, and disrupt the astrocyte-neuron communication in the cardiovascular regulatory centers of the brainstem and hypothalamus. The disturbance of excitatory amino acid transporter mediated glutamate homeostasis is specially concerning because it may intensify excitatory drive in autonomic circuits and sustain sympathoexcitation. In the context of obesity-associated hypertension, this review interconnects recent data to link metabolic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, central autonomic signaling, and astrocyte dysfunction. It also considers new therapeutic approaches targeted at restoring astrocytic balance. Targeting astrocyte-dependent pathways may provide a valuable supplementary strategy to address the neurogenic aspect of obesity-induced hypertension, even though several mechanistic questions remain unanswered.]]></description>

        <title><![CDATA[Familial risk for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and related behaviors in toddlerhood are preliminarily associated with altered frontoparietal development in infancy measured by functional near-infrared spectroscopy]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-20T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Original Research</category>
        <author>Meghna Krishnamurthy</author><author>Judith K. Morgan</author><author>Hendrik Santosa</author><author>Michelle A. Wilson</author><author>Theodore J. Huppert</author><author>Heather M. Joseph</author>
        <description><![CDATA[IntroductionAttention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common childhood neurodevelopmental disorder associated with impairments across the lifespan. Children with ADHD have been found to have delayed brain maturation. These delays may be present and detectable with functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) as early as infancy for children at familial risk for ADHD. The present study examined longitudinal changes in functional connectivity among infants at high and low familial risk for ADHD, and their association with ADHD-related behaviors in toddlerhood.MethodsParticipants were 44 infants, half at high familial risk for ADHD due to parental ADHD, assessed at 8-10 months and 12-14 months of age. fNIRS was used to measure hemodynamic activation in frontal and parietal regions during a low cognitive load task of attention. In toddlerhood, 18-30 months of age, parents rated ADHD-related behaviors using the Child Behavior Checklist.ResultsAcross the sample, longitudinal fNIRS analyses revealed increased frontal connectivity with a notable leftward shift between timepoints. High-risk children showed greater increases in frontoparietal connectivity relative to low-risk peers, with divergent trajectories observed in left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and right parietal connectivity. Greater parent-reported attention symptoms were broadly associated with increased frontoparietal connectivity.DiscussionAlthough most findings did not survive corrections for multiple comparisons, these findings suggest that familial ADHD risk and early ADHD-related behaviors may be associated with atypical frontoparietal and frontal network development across the first year of life, highlighting the potential of fNIRS as a tool for identifying early neural markers of ADHD risk that could be used to identify which infants could benefit from early preventative interventions.]]></description>

        <guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1986322</guid>

        <title><![CDATA[UAC-Net: a unified multi-task network with aggregated contextual attention and cross-layer fusion for brain tumor segmentation and classification]]></title>
        <pubdate>2026-10-20T00:00:00Z</pubdate>
        <category>Original Research</category>
        <author>Chuanqi Cai</author><author>Jincan Zhang</author><author>Dongyan Zhang</author><author>Wenna Chen</author><author>Xinghua Tan</author><author>Ganqin Du</author><author>Hongwei Jiang</author>
        <description><![CDATA[IntroductionAccurate segmentation and classification of brain tumors from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are critical for clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. However, existing methods typically treat these two tasks independently, failing to exploit their inherent complementarity, and often struggle to capture multi-scale contextual information essential for identifying small or irregular lesions.MethodsTo address these limitations, this paper proposes UAC-Net, a unified multi-task learning framework built upon a U-Net backbone that jointly optimizes tumor segmentation and classification through a shared encoder. Two core modules are introduced: (1) the Aggregated Contextual Attention (ACA) module, which enhances dynamic perception of critical lesion regions by combining local sliding-window attention with global downsampling attention across all encoder levels; and (2) the Adjacent Layer Multi-scale Feature Fusion (ALMFF) module, which enables cross-level feature interaction to enrich multi-scale representations. In the segmentation branch, ALMFF-fused features are progressively upsampled to achieve precise lesion localization; in the classification branch, ACA-enhanced deep features are aggregated via global average pooling to yield robust semantic representations for tumor typing.ResultsExperiments on two publicly available brain tumor MRI datasets demonstrate that UAC-Net achieves competitive and consistent performance compared with several representative methods. Specifically, UAC-Net obtains a classification accuracy of 98.53% and a Dice coefficient of 81.39% on the Figshare dataset, and achieves 99.07% classification accuracy and 86.61% Dice coefficient on the BRISC 2025 dataset.DiscussionThese findings suggest that integrating contextual attention and cross-layer feature fusion within a unified multi-task framework is a promising approach for joint brain tumor segmentation and classification.]]></description>
